title: Gestalt Therapy: Principles, Techniques and What Happens in a Session
summary: Learn what Gestalt therapy is, how it works, common techniques, what to expect in a session, and whether this approach may be the right fit for you.
body_markdown:
## Key Takeaways


- *Gestalt therapy is a humanistic approach that focuses on your present experience and the connections between your thoughts, emotions, body, and environment.*
- *Sessions can include active experiments, such as role-play or empty-chair work, to help you notice and explore your experience.*
- *Gestalt therapy may be available online, although the therapist and format you choose can affect how experiential exercises are adapted.*


You may have heard the term "Gestalt therapy" and wondered what it actually means. Or maybe you’re looking into different therapy approaches and want to understand one that focuses closely on what’s happening in the present moment. Gestalt therapy is experiential and collaborative, so you won't necessarily spend every session simply talking about what happened in the past. Instead, you may be invited to notice what you're feeling, thinking, sensing, or doing as you talk, and then explore that experience holistically with your therapist.


## What is Gestalt Therapy and How Did it Develop?


Gestalt therapy is a humanistic, experiential form of psychotherapy that focuses on your whole experience and what you're experiencing in the present moment. Fritz and Laura Perls developed the approach in the 1940s, and Paul Goodman and other early Gestalt therapists later shaped it.


> ***"While traditional Gestalt therapy is rarely practiced as a standalone modality today, many clinicians integrate its interventions into approaches such as CBT, ACT, and Emotion-Focused Therapy to help clients process emotions in real time." ‍***[- Talkspace Therapist, Reshawna Chapple, PhD, LCSW](https://www.talkspace.com/mental-health/conditions/author/reshawna-chapple/)


The word "Gestalt" is often associated with the idea of a whole that can't be fully understood by looking at its individual parts. The[American Psychological Association (APA)](https://www.apa.org/topics/psychotherapy/approaches) describes it as emphasizing "organismic holism," present-moment awareness, and accepting responsibility for yourself. In therapy, that translates into paying attention to how your thoughts, emotions, physical sensations, behavior, relationships, and environment fit together rather than treating each experience as an isolated symptom.


Gestalt therapy grew out of psychoanalytic thinking but moved away from making interpretations about a person's past the central focus of therapy. Instead, the approach is a form of[humanistic therapy](https://www.talkspace.com/online-therapy/humanistic-therapy/) and emphasizes awareness, direct experience, dialogue, and personal responsibility. The therapist and patient work together to explore what is happening between them and within the member in the present moment. That doesn't mean your past doesn't matter. Past experiences can come into a Gestalt therapy session, but your therapist may be interested in how you're experiencing and making sense of those experiences now.


## How Does Gestalt Therapy Work in the Here and Now?


Gestalt therapy works by helping you notice what you're experiencing in the present rather than focusing only on explaining why you feel a certain way. Your therapist may pay attention to your words, emotions, body language, physical sensations, and the relationship developing between you as you talk. One way to understand this is through "figure and ground." The figure is whatever stands out most strongly in your awareness at a particular moment, while the ground is the broader context surrounding it. What becomes the figure can change from moment to moment as your needs, feelings, and surroundings change.


According to an[overview of Gestalt principles by Yontef and Jacobs](https://gestalttherapy.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/intro_to_gestalt_therapy_2_2011.pdf) , Gestalt therapy also uses the idea of "unfinished business," which refers to feelings, needs, or experiences that haven't been fully expressed or resolved and may continue to affect how you respond in the present. Rather than assuming what those feelings mean, your therapist may help you notice how they show up right now.


For example, imagine telling your therapist, “I'm completely fine talking about my manager,” while repeatedly tapping your foot. Your therapist might say, “I notice your foot is moving quite a bit as you talk about your manager. What are you noticing right now?” The point isn't for the therapist to decide that you're anxious or angry. It's to allow you to notice something that may have been happening outside your immediate awareness. This is part of the approach's style. Rather than immediately interpreting an experience, you and your therapist explore what you can directly notice and describe about it.


The therapist is therefore an active participant in the relationship, but that doesn't mean they're directing every part of the session. Gestalt therapy emphasizes dialogue and collaboration, with your therapist helping you explore your experience while you remain an active participant in deciding what feels meaningful to examine.


## Which Gestalt Techniques and Exercises Might Your Therapist Use?


Gestalt therapy techniques are usually experiential exercises designed to help you become more aware of what you're thinking, feeling, sensing, or doing. They aren't a fixed checklist, and a Gestalt therapist may adapt an exercise to your goals, comfort level, and what emerges during a session. Some techniques you may encounter include:


1. **Empty-chair dialogue:** You imagine another person, a part of yourself, or a particular perspective sitting in an empty chair and speak to it directly. This can give you a way to express something you haven't been able to say aloud and explore the feelings that emerge. Empty-chair work has a long history in Gestalt therapy and is also used in other experiential approaches.
2. **Exaggeration:** Your therapist asks you to repeat or slightly exaggerate a gesture, movement, expression, or tone of voice. The goal isn't to perform or get the exercise “right,” but to help you notice what becomes clearer when you give an experience more attention.
3. **Role-play or enactment:** You act out a conversation, relationship dynamic, memory, or situation you're anticipating. For example, you could practice saying something you've been holding back while paying attention to what happens emotionally and physically as you say it.
4. **Guided imagery:** A therapist uses imagery to help you explore an emotion, situation, memory, or possibility in a more experiential way. Imagery isn't necessarily used in every Gestalt session, so your therapist should explain what they're inviting you to do and why.
5. **Dream work:** If a dream feels important to you, a Gestalt therapist would invite you to explore parts of the dream through dialogue, imagery, or enactment rather than focusing only on what the dream supposedly “means.” Contemporary Gestalt literature continues to describe dream exploration as part of the approach.


What is a Gestalt experiment?
In Gestalt therapy, an “experiment” is an in-session activity that gives you a chance to explore an experience directly rather than only talking about it. Your therapist may suggest one, but the exercise should be collaborative and adapted to what you're comfortable exploring.


## What to Expect During a Typical Gestalt Therapy Session


Therapy sessions are commonly held once a week for about 45 to 50 minutes, although this depends on your therapist, treatment plan, and needs. The exact structure of the session will also vary because Gestalt therapy isn't a rigid, manualized format. A session may look something like this:


1. **Check-in and connection.** You might begin by talking about what's been happening since your last session or what feels most important today. Your therapist may also ask what you're noticing as you begin the conversation.
2. **Present-moment exploration.** As you talk, you may be invited to slow down and notice emotions, physical sensations, changes in your voice or posture, or other parts of your experience. You don't have to arrive knowing exactly what you want to discuss.
3. **An experiential experiment, if it fits.** Your therapist may suggest an exercise such as role-play, empty-chair work, exaggerating a movement, or exploring a particular sensation. You can discuss the exercise with your therapist and decide whether it feels appropriate for you.
4. **Reflection and wrap-up.** Near the end of the session, you and your therapist can reflect on what you noticed and what you'd like to carry forward.


Your role is active throughout the process. Instead of simply answering questions while your therapist interprets what you're saying, you're encouraged to notice your own experience and take part in deciding what you want to explore. Personal responsibility is an important part of Gestalt therapy, but it isn't the same as blaming yourself for what you're experiencing. You may also feel a little awkward with experiential exercises at first, especially if you're used to therapy that mostly involves conversation. This is normal, and a good therapist will pace the work to meet you where you are.


> ***"When individuals become more comfortable, clinicians often see a shift from self-consciousness to curiosity and playfulness. Instead of analyzing feelings in the abstract, the individual engages directly with physical sensations in real time, steps fully into enactments, and begins to initiate experiential moments independently to deepen their own self-reflection."***[- Talkspace Therapist, Reshawna Chapple, PhD, LCSW](https://www.talkspace.com/mental-health/conditions/author/reshawna-chapple/)


## Is Gestalt Therapy Right for Your Needs and Goals?


Gestalt therapy may be a good fit if you want an active, present-focused approach that helps you explore emotions, relationships, and patterns as they show up in your life. It's best to think about the approach in terms of your goals, preferences, and the therapist's training rather than assuming it's the right fit for a particular diagnosis.


Recent research provides some encouraging but still limited evidence. In a 2025 study published in[Frontiers in Psychiatry](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41080786/) , 319 people with mood and/or anxiety disorders completed a Gestalt therapy program; participants showed statistically significant reductions in measures of anxiety, depression, and psychological distress after treatment. Because the study didn't establish that Gestalt therapy alone caused those changes, the findings should be viewed as promising rather than definitive evidence that the approach will work for everyone.


You might consider Gestalt therapy if you're dealing with:


- **Anxiety:** You want to become more aware of how anxious feelings show up in your thoughts, body, and interactions.
- **Depression:** You're interested in exploring your current emotional experience and patterns rather than focusing only on symptom reduction.
- **Relationship patterns:** You notice recurring patterns in how you connect, communicate, withdraw, or respond to other people to maintain[healthy boundaries in relationships](https://www.talkspace.com/blog/guide-setting-healthy-boundaries-relationships/) .
- **Self-esteem challenges:** You want to understand how you experience yourself and how your relationships or environment affect that experience.


Gestalt therapy may feel less aligned with your preferences if you're looking specifically for a highly structured, protocol-driven approach with clearly defined steps and homework. If you're more interested in exploring how the stories you tell about yourself shape your identity and experiences, you may also be interested in[narrative therapy](https://www.talkspace.com/blog/what-is-narrative-therapy/) , which takes a different approach to understanding your experiences.

## Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs)


### What is Gestalt therapy, and how does it work?


Gestalt therapy is a humanistic, experiential form of psychotherapy that focuses on your whole experience and what you're noticing in the present moment. It works through collaborative dialogue and may use exercises that help you explore emotions, physical sensations, relationships, and patterns as they happen.


### What techniques are commonly used in Gestalt therapy?


Common Gestalt therapy techniques include empty-chair dialogue, role-play, exaggeration, dream work, and other experiential exercises that can increase awareness. Your therapist may adapt or combine techniques based on what you're exploring, so you won't necessarily use the same exercises in every session.


### What happens during a Gestalt therapy session?


A Gestalt therapy session may begin with a check-in before moving into present-moment exploration and, when appropriate, an experiential exercise. Sessions are typically collaborative and active, with time at the end to reflect on what you noticed and what you'd like to explore next.


### Who can benefit from Gestalt therapy?


Gestalt therapy may appeal to people who want to explore their emotions, relationships, bodily sensations, and current experiences actively. Research into Gestalt therapy is still developing, so your goals, preferences, and the therapist's training are important when deciding whether it fits you.


### Can you do Gestalt therapy online?


Yes, Gestalt therapy online can be delivered through remote therapy formats. Through platforms like Talkspace, you can connect with licensed therapists, including those experienced in Gestalt approaches, who can adapt experiential and present-moment techniques to a virtual setting.
